supplements.name: Creatine monohydrate
supplements.timing: Any time; consistency matters more than timing
supplements.notes: Optional loading of 20 g/day for 5–7 days saturates muscle faster. Can raise serum creatinine without harming the kidneys, so tell whoever reads your labs.

supplements.name: Whey protein
supplements.dose: 20–40 g per serving, toward 1.6–2.2 g protein/kg/day in total
supplements.notes: Count it toward total daily protein rather than adding on top. Isolate suits lactose sensitivity.

supplements.name: Casein protein
supplements.notes: Slow digestion supports overnight muscle protein synthesis.

supplements.name: Plant protein blend
supplements.notes: Pea + rice blends match whey best; slightly higher servings make up for lower leucine.

supplements.name: Essential amino acids (EAAs)
supplements.notes: Useful when whole-protein intake is low; redundant if daily protein is adequate.

supplements.name: Branched-chain amino acids (BCAAs)
supplements.notes: Little benefit when total protein intake is adequate; EAAs or whole protein are better.

supplements.name: Leucine
supplements.notes: Most useful for older adults with low appetite.

supplements.name: HMB
supplements.notes: Benefits mainly in untrained or older people and during calorie restriction.

supplements.name: Caffeine
supplements.notes: Keep to about 400 mg/day for healthy adults and stop 8+ hours before bed. Avoid with arrhythmias, uncontrolled blood pressure or pregnancy beyond 200 mg.

supplements.name: L-theanine
supplements.timing: With caffeine, or in the evening
supplements.notes: Smooths caffeine jitters; 2:1 theanine to caffeine is common.

supplements.name: Beta-alanine
supplements.notes: Helps efforts of 1–4 minutes. Tingling (paresthesia) is harmless; sustained-release forms reduce it.

supplements.name: Citrulline malate
supplements.notes: Raises arginine and nitric oxide more reliably than arginine itself.

supplements.name: Sodium bicarbonate
supplements.notes: Gut upset is common; split doses or enteric capsules help. High sodium load.

supplements.name: Dietary nitrate (beetroot juice)
supplements.notes: Antibacterial mouthwash blocks the effect. Harmless red urine (beeturia).

supplements.name: Betaine (TMG)
supplements.notes: May slightly raise LDL in some people.

supplements.name: Taurine
supplements.notes: Ageing research in animals is promising; human data are early.

supplements.name: Carbohydrate (drinks, gels)
supplements.dose: 30–60 g/hour; up to 90 g/hour glucose+fructose for long events
supplements.notes: Train the gut beforehand to avoid GI distress.

supplements.name: Electrolytes (sodium)
supplements.dose: 300–600 mg sodium per hour of sweating
supplements.notes: Needs vary widely; a sweat test can personalise. Caution with high blood pressure or kidney disease.

supplements.name: Ketone esters
supplements.notes: Mixed performance results; GI upset and cost are common issues.

supplements.name: MCT oil
supplements.notes: Start low to avoid GI upset.

supplements.name: L-carnitine L-tartrate
supplements.notes: May reduce muscle damage markers. Raises TMAO, of uncertain significance.

supplements.name: Acetyl-L-carnitine
supplements.notes: Some evidence for mood and fatigue in older adults.

supplements.name: Tart cherry
supplements.dose: 480 mg extract or 30 ml concentrate twice daily
supplements.notes: Avoid constant use if you want maximal training adaptation from inflammation.

supplements.name: Collagen peptides
supplements.notes: Not a complete protein; don't count toward muscle-building protein.

supplements.name: Glutamine
supplements.notes: Little performance effect in healthy athletes.

supplements.name: Vitamin D3
supplements.dose: 1,000–4,000 IU daily, guided by 25(OH)D blood level
supplements.notes: Stay at or under 4,000 IU/day unless a clinician prescribes more. Retest after 8–12 weeks.

supplements.name: Vitamin K2 (MK-7)
supplements.notes: Do not take with warfarin unless your clinician agrees.

supplements.name: Vitamin C
supplements.notes: Mega-doses around training may blunt adaptations; kidney stone risk above 1 g/day.

supplements.name: Vitamin B12
supplements.notes: Important for vegans, people over 50 and metformin users. Treats deficiency only.

supplements.name: Folate (methylfolate)
supplements.notes: Essential before and during pregnancy. High doses can mask B12 deficiency.

supplements.name: B-complex
supplements.notes: Bright yellow urine from riboflavin is normal. Biotin interferes with many lab tests: stop 2–3 days before blood work.

supplements.name: Vitamin E
supplements.dose: 15 mg (22 IU) daily from food and supplements
supplements.notes: Avoid high-dose supplements: linked to higher prostate cancer risk and bleeding.

supplements.name: Multivitamin
supplements.notes: Large trials (COSMOS) found modest cognitive benefits in older adults.

supplements.name: Iron
supplements.dose: 18–65 mg elemental, only when ferritin or iron is low
supplements.timing: Alternate days, with vitamin C, away from coffee, tea and calcium
supplements.notes: Test before you take it. Excess iron is harmful, especially with hemochromatosis.

supplements.name: Magnesium glycinate
supplements.notes: Supplemental upper limit is 350 mg/day for most adults; above that diarrhoea is common. Caution with kidney disease.

supplements.name: Magnesium L-threonate
supplements.notes: Marketed for brain uptake; human trials are small.

supplements.name: Zinc
supplements.notes: Long-term intake above 40 mg/day causes copper deficiency.

supplements.name: Calcium
supplements.dose: Enough to reach 1,000–1,200 mg/day including diet
supplements.timing: No more than 500 mg at a time
supplements.notes: Food sources preferred. Separate from iron and thyroid medication.

supplements.name: Potassium citrate
supplements.dose: Food first; supplements are limited to 99 mg per pill in the US
supplements.notes: Dangerous with kidney disease, ACE inhibitors, ARBs or potassium-sparing diuretics.

supplements.name: Iodine
supplements.notes: Excess can trigger thyroid problems; avoid kelp mega-doses.

supplements.name: Selenium
supplements.notes: Upper limit 400 mcg/day. Two Brazil nuts ≈ 100–200 mcg.

supplements.name: Boron
supplements.notes: Small studies only.

supplements.name: Chromium picolinate
supplements.notes: Small effects on glucose at best.

supplements.name: Omega-3 (EPA + DHA)
supplements.notes: Above 3 g/day may raise atrial fibrillation and bleeding risk. Check with your clinician if you take blood thinners.

supplements.name: Plant sterols
supplements.notes: Lowers LDL by 6–12%.

supplements.name: Psyllium husk
supplements.dose: 5–10 g with a full glass of water
supplements.notes: Lowers LDL and blunts glucose spikes. Separate from medications by 2 hours.

supplements.name: Red yeast rice
supplements.notes: Contains monacolin K, identical to lovastatin, with the same risks. Product quality varies; a 2024 Japanese outbreak of kidney injury was linked to contaminated products. Don't combine with statins.

supplements.name: Aged garlic extract
supplements.notes: Modest blood pressure reduction. May increase bleeding with anticoagulants.

supplements.name: Cocoa flavanols
supplements.notes: The COSMOS trial suggested lower cardiovascular death. Chocolate is not an efficient source.

supplements.name: Coenzyme Q10 (ubiquinol)
supplements.notes: Often used with statins for muscle aches (mixed evidence). May reduce warfarin's effect.

supplements.name: Berberine
supplements.notes: Lowers glucose and LDL. Interacts with many drugs via CYP enzymes; avoid in pregnancy. GI upset common.

supplements.name: Alpha-lipoic acid
supplements.notes: Can lower blood sugar; monitor if diabetic.

supplements.name: Myo-inositol
supplements.notes: Best evidence is in PCOS.

supplements.name: Ceylon cinnamon
supplements.notes: Choose Ceylon: cassia contains coumarin, which can harm the liver.

supplements.name: Green tea extract (EGCG)
supplements.notes: Liver injury reported, mostly with fasting doses above 800 mg/day.

supplements.name: Curcumin (enhanced absorption)
supplements.notes: Rare liver injury, especially with piperine forms. Caution with anticoagulants and gallstones.

supplements.name: Ginger
supplements.notes: Helps nausea and mild muscle soreness.

supplements.name: Boswellia serrata
supplements.notes: Small trials in knee osteoarthritis are positive.

supplements.name: Glucosamine sulfate
supplements.notes: Mixed results for knee osteoarthritis. Shellfish-derived versions exist.

supplements.name: Chondroitin
supplements.notes: Often paired with glucosamine. May raise bleeding with warfarin.

supplements.name: MSM
supplements.notes: Small trials only.

supplements.name: Oral hyaluronic acid
supplements.notes: Small trials only.

supplements.name: Astaxanthin
supplements.notes: May reduce exercise-induced oxidative stress.

supplements.name: Lutein + zeaxanthin
supplements.notes: AREDS2 formula for macular degeneration.

supplements.name: N-acetylcysteine (NAC)
supplements.notes: Glutathione precursor. High doses around training may blunt adaptations.

supplements.name: Liposomal glutathione
supplements.notes: Oral absorption is debated.

supplements.name: Nicotinamide riboside (NR)
supplements.notes: Raises NAD+ in blood reliably; clinical benefits are not yet shown.

supplements.name: NMN
supplements.notes: Raises NAD+; human outcome data are limited. US regulatory status has changed over time.

supplements.name: Resveratrol
supplements.notes: Human results are inconsistent.

supplements.name: Quercetin
supplements.notes: Studied as a senolytic alongside other drugs. CYP interactions.

supplements.name: Fisetin
supplements.notes: Senolytic trials in humans are ongoing; results not yet established.

supplements.name: Spermidine
supplements.notes: Autophagy-related research; human trials are small.

supplements.name: Urolithin A
supplements.notes: Small trials show better muscle endurance and mitochondrial markers.

supplements.name: Calcium alpha-ketoglutarate (Ca-AKG)
supplements.notes: Mostly animal data; human trials ongoing.

supplements.name: Sulforaphane (broccoli sprout)
supplements.dose: 10–40 mg sulforaphane, or glucoraphanin with myrosinase
supplements.notes: Activates Nrf2 antioxidant pathways.

supplements.name: Pycnogenol (pine bark)
supplements.notes: Modest blood pressure and circulation effects.

supplements.name: Ashwagandha (root extract)
supplements.notes: Rare liver injury reported. Avoid in pregnancy; caution with thyroid disease.

supplements.name: Rhodiola rosea
supplements.notes: Can feel stimulating; avoid late in the day.

supplements.name: Panax ginseng
supplements.notes: May interact with warfarin and diabetes medication.

supplements.name: Tongkat ali
supplements.notes: Small trials; quality and contamination vary.

supplements.name: Fenugreek extract
supplements.notes: Can lower blood sugar. Maple-syrup body odour is harmless.

supplements.name: Maca
supplements.notes: Evidence mainly for libido.

supplements.name: Shilajit
supplements.notes: Unpurified products can contain heavy metals; buy third-party tested.

supplements.name: Saffron
supplements.notes: Several trials show mood benefits.

supplements.name: Lion's mane
supplements.notes: Small human trials.

supplements.name: Cordyceps
supplements.notes: Mixed results for VO2 max.

supplements.name: Reishi
supplements.notes: Rare liver toxicity; caution with anticoagulants.

supplements.name: Bacopa monnieri
supplements.notes: Effects build slowly; GI upset possible.

supplements.name: Alpha-GPC
supplements.notes: Choline source; may slightly raise TMAO.

supplements.name: Citicoline (CDP-choline)
supplements.notes: Attention benefits in small trials.

supplements.name: L-tyrosine
supplements.notes: Avoid with MAO inhibitors or hyperthyroidism.

supplements.name: 5-HTP
supplements.notes: Risk of serotonin syndrome with SSRIs, SNRIs, triptans or MAOIs: do not combine.

supplements.name: Melatonin
supplements.notes: Low doses work as well as high ones. Useful for jet lag and shift work.

supplements.name: Glycine
supplements.notes: Small trials show improved sleep quality.

supplements.name: Apigenin
supplements.notes: Chamomile compound; limited human data.

supplements.name: GABA
supplements.notes: Unclear whether it crosses into the brain.

supplements.name: Probiotics (strain-specific)
supplements.notes: Benefits depend on the exact strain and condition.

supplements.name: Bovine colostrum
supplements.notes: May reduce gut permeability during heavy training.

supplements.name: Digestive enzymes
supplements.notes: Lactase for lactose intolerance is the clearest use.

supplements.name: Elderberry
supplements.notes: May shorten colds slightly. Never eat raw berries.

supplements.name: Phosphatidylserine
supplements.notes: Some evidence for memory in older adults and for blunting cortisol after hard exercise.

supplements.name: Ginkgo biloba (EGb 761)
supplements.notes: Large trials (GEM) did not prevent dementia. Increases bleeding risk with anticoagulants and antiplatelets.

supplements.name: Huperzine A
supplements.notes: Acetylcholinesterase inhibitor with a long half-life. Can cause nausea, slow heart rate and muscle cramps; avoid with dementia drugs or before anaesthesia.

supplements.name: Uridine monophosphate
supplements.notes: Studied with omega-3 and choline (Souvenaid) in early Alzheimer's with modest effects.

supplements.name: Choline bitartrate
supplements.notes: Cheap choline source; less brain-targeted than alpha-GPC or citicoline. Fishy body odour at high doses.

supplements.name: Sulbutiamine
supplements.notes: Fat-soluble vitamin B1 derivative. Small studies on fatigue only.

supplements.name: Paraxanthine
supplements.notes: The main metabolite of caffeine; early trials suggest similar alertness with fewer jitters.

supplements.name: Theacrine
supplements.notes: Caffeine-like compound with less tolerance build-up in small studies. Can raise heart rate.

supplements.name: Gotu kola
supplements.notes: Rare liver injury reported.

supplements.name: Nicotinamide (vitamin B3)
supplements.notes: Reduced new skin cancers in high-risk people (ONTRAC). Doses above 3 g/day can harm the liver.

clinical.name: Metformin
clinical.mechanism: Lowers liver glucose output and improves insulin sensitivity.
clinical.evidence_text: TAME trial is testing it as an ageing drug. May blunt muscle and VO2 max gains from training in healthy people.
clinical.risks: GI upset, B12 deficiency, rare lactic acidosis (mainly kidney disease).
clinical.labs: HbA1c, fasting glucose, B12, kidney function (eGFR)

clinical.name: Semaglutide
clinical.uses: Type 2 diabetes, obesity, cardiovascular risk reduction
clinical.mechanism: Mimics GLP-1 to slow stomach emptying, cut appetite and improve insulin release.
clinical.evidence_text: SELECT trial: 20% fewer major cardiovascular events. 15% average weight loss in obesity trials.
clinical.risks: Nausea, vomiting, muscle and lean-mass loss, gallbladder disease, pancreatitis; avoid with personal/family history of medullary thyroid cancer.
clinical.labs: HbA1c, lipids, body composition (DEXA), kidney function

clinical.name: Tirzepatide
clinical.mechanism: Acts on both GIP and GLP-1 receptors to reduce appetite and improve glucose control.
clinical.evidence_text: SURMOUNT trials: about 20% average weight loss.
clinical.risks: Similar to semaglutide: GI effects, lean-mass loss, gallbladder and pancreatitis risk.

clinical.name: Liraglutide
clinical.mechanism: Daily GLP-1 agonist.
clinical.evidence_text: Less weight loss than weekly agents; cardiovascular benefit shown (LEADER).
clinical.risks: GI effects, gallbladder and pancreatitis risk.

clinical.name: Retatrutide
clinical.mechanism: Adds glucagon-receptor activity to raise energy expenditure.
clinical.evidence_text: Phase 2: about 24% weight loss at 48 weeks.
clinical.risks: Long-term safety unknown. Not legally available outside trials.

clinical.name: Empagliflozin
clinical.uses: Type 2 diabetes, heart failure, chronic kidney disease
clinical.mechanism: Makes the kidneys excrete glucose.
clinical.evidence_text: Strong heart and kidney protection; extended lifespan in male mice (ITP, canagliflozin).
clinical.risks: Genital infections, dehydration, rare ketoacidosis.
clinical.labs: Kidney function, glucose, ketones if unwell

clinical.name: Acarbose
clinical.mechanism: Slows carbohydrate digestion to blunt glucose spikes.
clinical.evidence_text: Extended lifespan in mice (ITP).
clinical.risks: Gas, bloating, diarrhoea.

clinical.name: Rapamycin (sirolimus)
clinical.status: Prescription (US) for transplant; longevity use is off-label
clinical.uses: Organ transplant rejection, some rare diseases
clinical.mechanism: Inhibits mTOR, a central nutrient-sensing growth pathway.
clinical.evidence_text: Most robust lifespan extension in mice. Human longevity trials (e.g. PEARL) are small and early.
clinical.risks: Immune suppression, mouth ulcers, raised lipids and glucose, impaired wound healing.
clinical.labs: Lipids, glucose, blood count, drug levels where applicable

clinical.name: Statins (e.g. rosuvastatin)
clinical.uses: High LDL and ApoB, cardiovascular prevention
clinical.mechanism: Blocks cholesterol production in the liver.
clinical.evidence_text: Decades of outcome data for heart attack and stroke prevention.
clinical.risks: Muscle aches, small rise in diabetes risk, rare liver injury.
clinical.labs: Lipid panel, ApoB, liver enzymes, CK if symptoms, HbA1c

clinical.name: Ezetimibe
clinical.mechanism: Blocks cholesterol absorption in the gut.
clinical.evidence_text: Adds to statins (IMPROVE-IT).
clinical.risks: Generally well tolerated.

clinical.name: PCSK9 inhibitors (evolocumab, alirocumab)
clinical.mechanism: Increases LDL receptor recycling in the liver.
clinical.evidence_text: Lowers LDL 50–60%; fewer cardiovascular events.
clinical.risks: Injection-site reactions; cost.

clinical.name: Bempedoic acid
clinical.mechanism: Blocks cholesterol production upstream of statins without muscle effects.
clinical.evidence_text: CLEAR Outcomes: fewer cardiovascular events.
clinical.risks: Raised uric acid, gout, tendon rupture (rare).

clinical.name: Low-dose aspirin
clinical.status: Over the counter; prevention use should be clinician-guided
clinical.uses: Secondary prevention of heart attack and stroke
clinical.mechanism: Irreversibly inhibits platelet COX-1.
clinical.evidence_text: No longer advised for routine primary prevention in older adults (ASPREE).
clinical.risks: Gastrointestinal and brain bleeding.

clinical.name: Telmisartan
clinical.mechanism: Blocks angiotensin II; partial PPAR-gamma activity.
clinical.evidence_text: Strong blood pressure outcome data.
clinical.risks: High potassium, dizziness, kidney effects; not in pregnancy.

clinical.name: Testosterone replacement therapy
clinical.mechanism: Replaces testosterone when the body makes too little.
clinical.evidence_text: Improves symptoms in confirmed deficiency. TRAVERSE trial: no increase in major cardiovascular events in men with hypogonadism.
clinical.risks: Raised haematocrit, infertility and testicular shrinkage, acne, sleep apnoea, prostate effects. Use without a diagnosis is illegal and unsafe.
clinical.labs: Total and free testosterone, haematocrit, PSA, estradiol, lipids

clinical.name: Menopausal hormone therapy
clinical.mechanism: Replaces estrogen (plus progestogen if you have a uterus).
clinical.evidence_text: Best for symptoms when started within 10 years of menopause or before age 60.
clinical.risks: Blood clots and stroke (lower with skin patches), breast cancer risk with combined therapy.

clinical.name: Levothyroxine
clinical.mechanism: Replaces thyroxine (T4).
clinical.evidence_text: Standard treatment for deficiency only.
clinical.risks: Over-treatment causes arrhythmia and bone loss.

clinical.name: DHEA
clinical.status: Dietary supplement in the US; prescription or banned elsewhere; banned in sport (WADA)
clinical.mechanism: Converted into testosterone and estrogen.
clinical.evidence_text: Benefits in healthy people are inconsistent.
clinical.risks: Acne, hair loss, hormone-sensitive cancer concerns.

clinical.name: Finasteride
clinical.uses: Male pattern hair loss, enlarged prostate
clinical.mechanism: Lowers DHT.
clinical.evidence_text: Effective for hair loss.
clinical.risks: Sexual side effects, mood changes; lowers PSA readings.

clinical.name: Minoxidil
clinical.uses: Hair loss; oral form for blood pressure
clinical.mechanism: Prolongs the hair growth phase.
clinical.evidence_text: Effective for hair loss.
clinical.risks: Scalp irritation; oral form can cause fluid retention and fast heart rate.

clinical.name: Tadalafil
clinical.uses: Erectile dysfunction, enlarged prostate, pulmonary hypertension
clinical.mechanism: Increases blood flow by boosting cGMP.
clinical.evidence_text: Approved indications only; no proven performance benefit.
clinical.risks: Headache, flushing; dangerous with nitrates.

clinical.name: Low-dose naltrexone
clinical.uses: Off-label for fibromyalgia, some autoimmune conditions
clinical.mechanism: Brief opioid-receptor blockade with possible anti-inflammatory effects.
clinical.evidence_text: Small trials only.
clinical.risks: Vivid dreams, insomnia; blocks opioid painkillers.

clinical.name: Modafinil
clinical.status: Prescription, controlled (US Schedule IV); banned in sport (WADA)
clinical.uses: Narcolepsy, shift-work disorder, sleep apnoea fatigue
clinical.mechanism: Increases dopamine and other wake-promoting signals.
clinical.evidence_text: Modest cognitive effects in sleep-deprived people.
clinical.risks: Insomnia, headache, rare severe skin reactions; reduces hormonal contraceptive effect.

clinical.name: Dasatinib + quercetin
clinical.status: Dasatinib is a prescription cancer drug; senolytic use is experimental
clinical.mechanism: Clears senescent cells in animal models.
clinical.evidence_text: Small human pilot studies only.
clinical.risks: Dasatinib: low blood counts, fluid around the lungs, bleeding.

clinical.name: Sildenafil
clinical.mechanism: Increases blood flow by boosting cGMP.
clinical.evidence_text: Approved indications only.
clinical.risks: Headache, visual changes; dangerous with nitrates.

clinical.name: Armodafinil
clinical.status: Prescription, controlled (US Schedule IV); banned in sport (WADA)
clinical.uses: Narcolepsy, shift-work disorder, residual sleepiness in sleep apnoea
clinical.mechanism: The longer-acting R-isomer of modafinil; increases dopamine signalling.
clinical.evidence_text: Similar to modafinil: improves wakefulness in sleep-deprived people; small effects in rested healthy people.
clinical.risks: Insomnia, headache, anxiety, rare serious skin reactions; reduces hormonal contraceptive effectiveness.

clinical.name: Adrafinil
clinical.status: Not approved in the US; withdrawn in France; banned in sport (WADA)
clinical.mechanism: Converted to modafinil in the liver.
clinical.evidence_text: Little direct human research.
clinical.risks: Raised liver enzymes with regular use; same risks as modafinil.

clinical.name: Methylphenidate
clinical.status: Prescription, controlled (US Schedule II); banned in competition (WADA)
clinical.mechanism: Blocks dopamine and noradrenaline reuptake.
clinical.evidence_text: Clear benefit in ADHD. In healthy people, effects are small and people tend to overestimate them.
clinical.risks: Raised heart rate and blood pressure, insomnia, appetite loss, dependence and misuse; dangerous with heart conditions.

clinical.name: Amphetamine salts
clinical.status: Prescription, controlled (US Schedule II); banned in competition (WADA)
clinical.mechanism: Releases dopamine and noradrenaline.
clinical.evidence_text: Clear benefit in ADHD; limited and mixed benefit for healthy people.
clinical.risks: Raised heart rate and blood pressure, insomnia, anxiety, psychosis at high doses, dependence; cardiac risk.

clinical.name: Piracetam
clinical.status: Not approved in the US and cannot be sold as a supplement; prescription in parts of Europe
clinical.mechanism: Thought to modulate AMPA receptors and membrane fluidity; not fully understood.
clinical.evidence_text: No convincing benefit in healthy adults. Mixed results in older people with cognitive impairment.
clinical.risks: Agitation, insomnia, increased bleeding with anticoagulants.

clinical.name: Aniracetam
clinical.status: Not approved in the US; FDA has warned sellers
clinical.mechanism: AMPA receptor modulator.
clinical.evidence_text: Very limited human evidence.
clinical.risks: Anxiety, headache, insomnia. Product quality is unregulated.

clinical.name: Phenylpiracetam
clinical.status: Prescription in Russia; not approved in the US; banned in competition (WADA)
clinical.mechanism: Racetam with stimulant properties.
clinical.evidence_text: Mostly Russian-language studies; little independent data.
clinical.risks: Insomnia, irritability, raised blood pressure, tolerance.

clinical.name: Noopept
clinical.status: Prescription/OTC in Russia; not approved in the US; FDA has warned sellers
clinical.mechanism: Proposed to raise BDNF and NGF; acts on AMPA receptors.
clinical.evidence_text: Small, mostly Russian-language trials.
clinical.risks: Headache, irritability, sleep problems. Unregulated product quality.

clinical.name: Memantine
clinical.mechanism: Blocks excessive glutamate signalling.
clinical.evidence_text: Modest benefit in Alzheimer's; no shown benefit in healthy people.
clinical.risks: Dizziness, headache, confusion.

clinical.name: Nicotine (replacement therapy)
clinical.status: Gum, lozenges and patches are OTC (US) for smoking cessation; on WADA's monitoring programme, not banned
clinical.mechanism: Activates nicotinic acetylcholine receptors.
clinical.evidence_text: Improves attention and fine motor speed in small studies, including non-smokers.
clinical.risks: Highly addictive; raises heart rate and blood pressure; nausea. Avoid in pregnancy and heart disease.

clinical.name: Vinpocetine
clinical.status: Sold as a supplement in the US; FDA warns against use in pregnancy; prescription in some countries
clinical.mechanism: PDE1 inhibitor that may increase brain blood flow.
clinical.evidence_text: Weak, older trials.
clinical.risks: Miscarriage and fetal harm risk; low blood pressure; bleeding with anticoagulants.

clinical.name: Phenibut
clinical.status: Not approved in the US; FDA has warned against it; controlled in several countries
clinical.mechanism: Acts like baclofen at GABA-B receptors.
clinical.evidence_text: Little quality evidence.
clinical.risks: Rapid tolerance, dependence and severe withdrawal (seizures, psychosis); dangerous with alcohol or sedatives. Poison-centre calls have risen sharply.

clinical.name: Tianeptine
clinical.status: Not approved in the US; FDA has issued repeated warnings; prescription in some countries
clinical.mechanism: Opioid-receptor agonist at higher exposure.
clinical.evidence_text: Effective antidepressant at prescribed doses where approved.
clinical.risks: Opioid-like dependence, withdrawal, overdose and death have been reported with US gas-station products.

peptides.name: Tesamorelin
peptides.sport: Prohibited at all times (WADA S2, peptide hormones and growth factors)
peptides.uses: Reducing excess abdominal fat in HIV-associated lipodystrophy
peptides.mechanism: Stimulates the pituitary to release growth hormone, raising IGF-1.
peptides.evidence_text: Randomised trials show less visceral fat and liver fat in HIV. Not studied as a performance or anti-ageing drug.
peptides.risks: Joint pain, fluid retention, raised blood sugar, injection-site reactions; avoid with active cancer.

peptides.name: Sermorelin
peptides.status: Previously FDA-approved; brand discontinued in the US in 2008; sometimes compounded
peptides.sport: Prohibited at all times (WADA S2, peptide hormones and growth factors)
peptides.evidence_text: Older paediatric data; little adult outcome data.
peptides.risks: Flushing, headache, injection-site reactions; long-term adult safety not established.

peptides.name: Bremelanotide (PT-141)
peptides.sport: Prohibited at all times (WADA S0, non-approved substances) outside approved medical use
peptides.uses: Low sexual desire in premenopausal women
peptides.mechanism: Activates melanocortin-4 receptors in the brain.
peptides.evidence_text: Modest improvement in desire in phase 3 trials.
peptides.risks: Nausea (common), flushing, temporary rise in blood pressure, skin darkening.

peptides.name: Afamelanotide
peptides.sport: Prohibited at all times (WADA S0, non-approved substances) outside approved medical use
peptides.mechanism: Activates melanocortin-1 receptors to increase skin melanin.
peptides.evidence_text: Increased pain-free sun exposure in trials.
peptides.risks: Nausea, headache, darkening of moles; needs skin checks.

peptides.name: Setmelanotide
peptides.sport: Prohibited at all times (WADA S0, non-approved substances) outside approved medical use
peptides.uses: Obesity from specific rare genetic conditions
peptides.mechanism: Restores appetite signalling in MC4R pathway defects.
peptides.evidence_text: Significant weight loss in those genetic conditions only.
peptides.risks: Skin darkening, nausea, depression and suicidal thoughts.

peptides.name: Teriparatide / abaloparatide
peptides.sport: Prohibited at all times (WADA S2, peptide hormones and growth factors)
peptides.mechanism: Intermittent PTH signalling builds new bone.
peptides.risks: Dizziness, leg cramps, raised calcium. Usually limited to two years.

peptides.name: Oxytocin
peptides.status: Prescription (US) for labour induction; nasal use is off-label/experimental
peptides.sport: Prohibited at all times (WADA S2, peptide hormones and growth factors)
peptides.mechanism: Acts on oxytocin receptors in the uterus and brain.
peptides.evidence_text: Social-behaviour effects of nasal oxytocin are inconsistent and many early findings did not replicate.

peptides.name: Thymosin alpha-1
peptides.status: Approved in some countries (Zadaxin) for hepatitis B and as an immune adjuvant; not approved in the US
peptides.sport: Prohibited at all times (WADA S0, non-approved substances)
peptides.uses: Hepatitis B, immune support (outside the US)
peptides.evidence_text: Mixed results; some trials in sepsis and hepatitis.
peptides.risks: Injection-site reactions; generally well tolerated in trials.

peptides.name: Elamipretide (SS-31)
peptides.status: FDA accelerated approval (2025) for Barth syndrome only; otherwise investigational
peptides.sport: Prohibited at all times (WADA S0, non-approved substances) outside approved medical use
peptides.mechanism: Binds cardiolipin in the inner mitochondrial membrane to stabilise energy production.
peptides.evidence_text: Benefit in Barth syndrome; trials in mitochondrial myopathy and heart failure missed main endpoints.

peptides.name: Cerebrolysin
peptides.status: Approved in parts of Europe and Asia; not approved in the US
peptides.sport: Prohibited at all times (WADA S0, non-approved substances)
peptides.evidence_text: Systematic reviews show little or no benefit after stroke.

peptides.name: Cagrilintide (with semaglutide: CagriSema)
peptides.sport: Prohibited at all times (WADA S0, non-approved substances)
peptides.mechanism: Mimics amylin to increase fullness; combined with semaglutide.
peptides.risks: GI side effects similar to GLP-1 drugs; long-term safety still being studied.

peptides.name: Kisspeptin
peptides.status: Research use in fertility trials; not approved
peptides.sport: Prohibited at all times (WADA S2, peptide hormones and growth factors)
peptides.mechanism: Stimulates GnRH, LH and FSH release.
peptides.evidence_text: Human research studies in reproductive medicine show reliable LH release.
peptides.risks: Research-setting only; effects on long-term fertility unknown.

peptide_guide.title: What counts as a peptide
peptide_guide.text: Chains of 2–50 amino acids. Insulin, GLP-1 drugs, oxytocin and parathyroid hormone analogues are peptides.

peptide_guide.title: What's included
peptide_guide.text: Peptides approved as medicines somewhere, and peptides in registered clinical trials. Unapproved 'research peptides' are not included.

peptide_guide.title: Research peptides
peptide_guide.text: Products labelled 'not for human consumption' have no approval, usually no controlled human data, and testing regularly finds wrong amounts, other substances and contamination. Almost all are banned in sport.

peptide_guide.title: Talking to a clinician
peptide_guide.text: Approved peptides are prescribed, dosed and monitored by a clinician. Bring this page to an appointment to discuss options and which labs to track.
